chapters.headline: POETICAL
chapters.text: First up — Page 1, Column 1. POETICAL. In the whole range of English fugitive poetry, we have met with few pieces of deeper pathos, or tenderer feeling, than this, by Alaric Watts. It breathes the very soul of devoted affection.

chapters.headline: FOR EVER THINE
chapters.text:
FOR EVER THINE. For ever thine, whate'er this heart betide,
For ever thine, where'er our lot be cast
Fate, that may rob us of all wealth beside,
Shall leave us love till life itself be past.
The world may wrong us we will brave its hate;
False friends may change, and falser hopes decline;
Though bowed by cankering care, we'll smile at Fate
Since thou art mine, beloved, and I am thine!
Later stanzas: Time's frosty blossoms; youth's glow; evening's dewy hour; Fashion's heartless throng; the boisterous crowd and sparkling wine. Closing refrain: My thoughts, my thoughts are thine, for ever thine.

chapters.headline: THE SHEPHERD'S LOVE
chapters.text:
THE SHEPHERD'S LOVE. BY J. A. DANA.
A rustic maiden (Jeanie, "the flower o' Ettrick") trips over the lea; a young shepherd (Willie) waits behind a ruined wall with his dog Wallace. They were to have been one next Michaelmas on the Ellaay farm; a richer man has outbid him; he has engaged for the Indies, the ship sailing to-morrow.

chapters.headline: Page 1, Columns 2-4
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 1, Columns 2-4. Page 1, Columns 2-4. The Dana tale continues: two years' absence promised; Jeanie's aged father; she contemplates marrying a "staid farmer of the border" to secure her father's comfort. Wedding morning at the kirk; a chaise at the door; the returned shepherd, William Sanford, claims a prior betrothal. He had been shipwrecked, reached India, rose in the service; letters miscarried. The first bridegroom resigns; the minister unites Jeanie and her returned lover.
Short fillers at the foot of column 4 (a misspelt love-letter joke; accidental sorrows; New Orleans cypress trunks under the gas-works; Kendall on San Antonio; a landlady's "excellent table"; Commercial Bank of New York exploded; Princeton gun; a Toronto child born with three eyes; Mobile cucumbers; a bill to reduce federal salaries).

chapters.headline: WHIGGERY EXPOSED
chapters.text:
WHIGGERY EXPOSED. Whig falsification / dissembling of Henry Clay; the democratic party the only true friends to American industry; consistency of Martin Van Buren, the People's Candidate.
The piece denies that the Whig party favor a protective tariff in the interest of honest industry; the present law is called prohibitory (iron, glass, sugars, woollens, cottons). Clay letters are quoted against a prohibitory tariff: Branham and Bledsoe, Eatonville, Georgia, July 28, 1842; Mr. Merriwether of Georgia, Oct. 2, 1843; F. S. Bronson, Oct. 13, 1843; New Orleans letter to Virginia Whigs, Jan. 2d, 1844; extra-session speech; Tennessee Agriculturist. Southern Clay papers (Mr. Rives of Virginia; Richmond Whig) are cited as calling Clay more of a free-trade man than Van Buren.
The article runs onto page 2.

chapters.headline: WHIGGERY EXPOSED
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Columns 1-5. WHIGGERY EXPOSED. continues.
Northern Whig testimony: New York Tribune / Courier and Enquirer; Savannah Republican; Daniel Webster against a large tariff. Charge that northern Whigs conceal a prohibitory policy while Clay writes free-trade letters to the South.
Van Buren letter, Albany, February 20 or 9, 184[3], to a Virginia friend (Richmond Enquirer): decided disapprobation of the Tariff act of the last session, "as well in respect to the principles upon which it is founded, as to its details."
Long extract: MR. VAN BUREN'S TARIFF OPINIONS. From Mr. Van Buren's Indiana Letter. Constitutional power to encourage domestic interests; opposition to oppressing any section; agricultural interest protected mainly by climate and soil; mechanics and laborers the greatest sufferers by high protective tariffs; incidental protection from a revenue tariff (about 20 per cent plus charges) is all the legislative favor that can be conferred without injustice; "OF THE CONSTITUTIONAL POWER to make DISCRIMINATIONS, I HAVE NO DOUBT." Wages of industry: "The workingman is to society, what the mainmast is to a ship."
Andrew Jackson letter, Washington City, April 26, 1824: climate and soil for hemp and wool; a careful and judicious tariff to pay the national debt and afford defence.
Close: MARTIN VAN BUREN IS, EMPHATICALLY, THE PEOPLE'S CANDIDATE.
A yankee is starting a plan to cause machinery to be driven by lightning.

chapters.headline: EDITED BY L. HARPER
chapters.text:
EDITED BY L. HARPER. "HE IS A FREEMAN WHOM THE TRUTH MAKES FREE."
KAY-diz, OHIO:
THURSDAY MORNING, APRIL 4, 1844.
The Tariff Position of Mr. Clay and Mr. Van Buren -- An important article -- Read and circulate.
The long tariff article on the first two pages is credited as found in the Statesman, not under the editorial head. Federal orators "still harping" on the tariff; young federal dandies in Russian hats, English broadcloth, French boots, talking to farmers about a Protective Tariff. Democrats are called the real friends of a tariff that benefits the whole people.

chapters.headline: "THE DEFEATED CANDIDATE."
chapters.text: Next up — Page 3, Column 2. "THE DEFEATED CANDIDATE.". Whigs call Van Buren the defeated candidate; Clay has been defeated three several times. Van Buren in 1840 received a much larger vote than any other candidate. Organized fraud and pipe-laying; infamous stories (standing army; late war; elective franchise; mechanic's wages; tax on chickens; Queen of England; the Pope; French bedsteads; gold spoons). Honest democrats returning; mechanics who were charmed by "two dollars a day and roast beef."

chapters.text:
DEMOCRATS ORGANIZE!. Our friends in Green, German and Stock have commenced the work of organizing the respective townships. Will not the democracy of all the other townships in Harrison county follow the example?

chapters.headline: Married
chapters.text:
Married. On the 11th inst., by the Rev. John Rea, George S. Atkinson, Merchant, of Harrisville, O., to Matilda Simeral, of Union Vale.
On the 27th ult., by Rev. Wesley Smith, Mr. Thomas Williams of Flushing, to Miss Rachel Brokaw of New Athens in this county.
On Wednesday (yesterday) morning, by Rev. Joseph Clokey, Mr. John P. Kilgore, to Miss Mary S. daughter of the Rev. Alexander Wilson, all of KAY-diz.
(ALTO of the officiant in the first notice is "Ren"; of the second bride "Dkokaw"; of the third groom "Kil-iorf." Page-image crops were read as Rea, Brokaw, and Kilgore. "11th inst." is printed as such on an April 4 number.)
Editorial note on the Kilgore cake brought into the sanctum: the editor was wondering if Mr. Van Buren would invite him to a seat in his cabinet on the fourth of March next. "Our friend Kilgore and his amiable bride have our heartiest thanks." Verse: "As calm as lakes that sleep / In starry moonlight glistening." Ed. Sentinel.

(ALTO of the officiant in the first notice is "Ren"; of the second bride "Dkokaw"; of the third groom "Kil-iorf." Page-image crops were read as Rea, Brokaw, and Kilgore. "11th inst." is printed as such on an April 4 number.)
Editorial note on the Kilgore cake brought into the sanctum: the editor was wondering if Mr. Van Buren would invite him to a seat in his cabinet on the fourth of March next. "Our friend Kilgore and his amiable bride have our heartiest thanks." Verse: "As calm as lakes that sleep / In starry moonlight glistening." Ed. Sentinel.

chapters.headline: OBITUARY
chapters.text: OBITUARY. Departed this life at his residence, in KAY-diz township, on the 9th of March, Mr. Francis Grove, in the 63d year of his age. Native of York county, Penn.; emigrated with his family to this county in the spring of 1833. Highly respected as a neighbor and as a citizen; for many years a ruling elder in the Associate Presbyterian church. Died in the exercise of the faith which he professed. A widow and a numerous family of children. Signed L.

A notice from the advertising columns. LAST NOTICE. Book accounts to officers after the fifteenth of March. Leaving KAY-diz the first of April. WM. BENNETT. KAY-diz, Feb. 29th, 1844.
Flax seed wanted -- P. R. K. BROTHERSON.
chapters.read:
